summary: You draft and play cards from an asymmetric civilization deck, moving cards through hand, discard, and achievement zones to build an engine that produces resources, unrest management, and victory points. It plays like efficient multiplayer solitaire: turns are quick and mostly non-interactive, with the tension coming from managing your own deck's growth and timing your Revolt to lock in bonuses before the game ends.
praised: high card quality and strong asymmetry between civilizations
excellent solo mode with civilization-specific AI opponents
satisfying, tight engine-building within a small card pool
very replayable due to variable setup and many civ combinations
fully compatible with Imperium: Classics, doubling the civ pool
criticised: dense keyword/iconography learning curve on first plays
some civilizations feel notably stronger or weaker than others
low direct interaction can feel like solitaire at a shared table
end-game achievement scoring can be fiddly to track
some Legends civs seen as more complex/fiddly than Classics ones

interaction.kind: mostly parallel play with light open drafting for shared cards

scoring.why: final score combines achievement track bonuses, leftover resources, and points printed on played cards, so efficient long-term engine building wins

similar: Through the Ages: A New Story of Civilization
